puzzles.title: Based Blue Lightning
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: This one is fairly tricky, especially if you're new to region sum lines. Here is a quick explaination of region sum lines:
Each time a region sum line crosses from one 3x3 box to another, it splits the digits in the two boxes into segments of the same sum.
For example, the long blue line at the top of the puzzle is split into the following six segments:
Note that two of these segments just contain a single cell, i.e., r3c6 and r4c7. This implies two things:
1. These two cells must contain the same digit.
2. The longer segments each cannot sum to more than 9, because otherwise the two single-cell segments would need to contain digits greater than 9, which is impossible.
Note also that the minimum sum of any 3-cell segment is 6, i.e., the sum of the digits 1, 2, and 3. This implies that r3c6 and r4c7 cannot be lower than 6, so they must be from the set {6, 7, 8, 9}.

puzzles.title: Almost Time(s)
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: I'll be sticking to posting 6x6 puzzles for a bit, since they're quicker and more approachable, which is probably better for a daily puzzle in your social feed.
This one is a follow-up to the previous puzzle, sticking with the same theme of region sum lines.
Remember, the smallest possible sum of any 3-cell segment is 6, i.e., the sum of the digits 1, 2, and 3.

puzzles.title: Number Go Up
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: Time to introduce some new rules! The key to solving this one is in the interaction between the German Whispers (green lines) and the Killer Cages (dashed boxes).
Here's a hint: in 6x6 sudoku, every row, column and 2x3 box sums to 21, which should help you place your first digit in column 4.
If you get stuck, tag @webthe3rd.eth and I'll give you another hint!

puzzles.title: Shoot the Gap
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: This puzzle introduces just one extra rule: arrow sums! The digits along each arrow must sum to the value in the arrow's attached circle. Two of the arrow sums are given, so for those you just need to deduce which digits sum to the given values.

Here's a hint: the blue arrow doesn't have a sum given, but the arrow is 5 cells long, so the digit in the circle can't be less than 5. In 6x6 sudoku the maximum digit is 6, so there are only two possible sums for the blue arrow! (Though when you think about it, there's really only one possibility)
If you get stuck, tag @webthe3rd.eth and I'll give you another hint!

puzzles.title: Icy Hot
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: Another new puzzle, another new rule: thermometers! The digits along each thermometer must increase in value from the bulb to the tip. For example, r3c2 must be greater than r3c1, r3c3 greater than r3c2, and so on up to r3c6.

Hint: The two long thermometers in the middle each take up an entire row, so they must contain the digits 1 through 6 in order. This should help you place your first digits and complete boxes 3 and 4!
If you get stuck, tag @webthe3rd.eth and I'll give you another hint!

puzzles.title: The Answer
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: Today's puzzle sees the return of arrow sums, but with a twist: this time, the arrow has a two-digit sum!
Remember, the sum of the digits 1 through 6 is 21, so you can automatically deduce the sum of the arrow. If you get stuck, tag @webthe3rd.eth and I'll give you another hint!

puzzles.title: Forty Two Skidoo
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: Today's puzzle introduces a new rule! Known as Kropki dots in variant sudoku circles, these black and white dots remind me of the game Go.

These dots affect pairs of adjacent cells, which are often referred to as 'dominoes'. Usually not all possible dots are given, which we would call a 'partial Kropki puzzle'. This one also features the negative constraint however, which means the absence of a dot can be just as informative as one's presence.

puzzles.title: Forty Two Skidoo Part Two
puzzles.author: WEBthe3rd
notes: Expanding on the theme of the previous puzzle, this one features the return of the black Kropki dot, along with another type of dominoes: XV pairs, which are pairs of cells that add up to either 10 (X) or 5 (V).

Unlike the previous puzzle, not all possible Kropki dots are given, but the negative constraint is still present for XV pairs. That means that if you don't see an X or a V between two adjacent cells, then the digits must not add up to either 10 or 5.

Here's a hint: in 6x6 sudoku, the only way to add two adjacent digits to make 10 is to use the digits 4 and 6. So wherever you see an X between two cells, you can pencil in the digits 4 and 6 as the only candidates.
If you get stuck, tag @webthe3rd.eth and I'll give you another hint!
